claim: IRF5-deficient mice show markedly enhanced metastasis of B16F1 melanoma cells in the lungs.
source: As shown in Figure 1A,B, we observed markedly enhanced metastasis of B16 cells in the lungs of mutant mice deficient in the Irf5 gene (hereafter IRF5-deficient mice).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B demonstrating increased lung metastasis in IRF5-deficient mice.

claim: Massive tumor growth was observed when B16 cells were subcutaneously injected into IRF5-deficient mice.
source: Massive tumor growth was also observed when B16 cells were subcutaneously injected into the mutant mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Whole splenocytes from IRF5-deficient mice show decreased killing activity against B16 cells compared to wild-type mice.
source: When whole splenocytes, of which about 3% are resting NK cells in both wild-type (WT) and IRF5-deficient mice (Takaoka et al., 2005), were subjected to an in vitro killing assay (Brunner et al., 1968) (51Cr release assay) for B16 cells, a notable decrease of killing activity was observed in those from IRF5-deficient mice (Figure 1C; left panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro killing assays shown in Figure 1C and cites previous work (Takaoka et al., 2005; Brunner et al., 1968).

claim: Purified NK cells from IRF5-deficient mice show normal killing activity against B16 cells.
source: Interestingly, however, when NK cells were purified from these splenocytes and then subjected to the killing assay, the lack of IRF5 did not affect the NK activity (Figure 1C; middle panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro killing assays shown in Figure 1C.

claim: NK cell depletion from splenocytes abrogates killing activity against B16 cells in both wild-type and IRF5-deficient mice.
source: Since the killing activity is entirely abrogated by NK cell depletion in both WT and mutant splenocytes (Figure 1C; right panel), these results indicate there is a critical contribution of non-NK cells within the total splenocyte population for which IRF5 is critical for the full-blown killing activity of NK cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro killing assays shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Non-NK cells within the total splenocyte population critically contribute to the full-blown killing activity of NK cells in an IRF5-dependent manner.
source: Since the killing activity is entirely abrogated by NK cell depletion in both WT and mutant splenocytes (Figure 1C; right panel), these results indicate there is a critical contribution of non-NK cells within the total splenocyte population for which IRF5 is critical for the full-blown killing activity of NK cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing that NK cell depletion abrogates killing activity and that IRF5-deficient splenocytes have reduced activity.

claim: Co-culture of purified NK cells with CD11c+ dendritic cells or CD11b+ macrophages results in a dose-dependent increase in NK killing activity against B16 cells.
source: Consistent with this notion, when purified NK cells were co-cultured with CD11c+ DCs and macrophage-enriched CD11b+ cells from splenocytes (hereafter referred to as co-culture assay), a dose-dependent and significant increase in NK killing activity was observed, whereas T or B lymphocytes had no such effect (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from co-culture assays shown in Figure 1D.

claim: T or B lymphocytes do not enhance NK killing activity against B16 cells in co-culture assays.
source: Consistent with this notion, when purified NK cells were co-cultured with CD11c+ DCs and macrophage-enriched CD11b+ cells from splenocytes (hereafter referred to as co-culture assay), a dose-dependent and significant increase in NK killing activity was observed, whereas T or B lymphocytes had no such effect (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from co-culture assays shown in Figure 1D.

claim: CD11b+ or CD11c+ cells from IRF5-deficient mice show reduced ability to enhance NK killing activity compared to those from wild-type mice.
source: Of note, a marked reduction of the NK killing activity was observed when CD11b+ or CD11c+ cells from IRF5-deficient mice were used in lieu of those from WT mice in the co-culture assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from co-culture assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Both dendritic cells and macrophages participate in the enhancement of NK cell-mediated killing activity.
source: The enhancement of NK killing activity was also made in another co-culture assay, wherein CD8+CD11c+, CD8−CD11c+, or CD11c−CD11b+ cells purified from splenocytes were used, indicating that both DCs and macrophages participate in the enhancement of NK cell-mediated killing activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from co-culture assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: IRF5 expression specifically in bone marrow-derived cells critically contributes to the suppression of B16 tumor cell metastasis.
source: To examine the contribution of immune cells, we next conducted bone marrow transplantation and found that IRF5 expression specifically in bone marrow-derived cells critically contributes to the suppression of the tumor cell metastasis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from bone marrow transplantation experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Marked B16 lung metastasis was not observed in mice deficient in T and B lymphocyte development.
source: Since the marked B16 lung metastasis was not observed in mice deficient in T and B lymphocyte development (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), we next examined the contribution of IRF5 in anti-tumor innate immune response, wherein NK cells are best known for their direct anti-tumor cytotoxicity (Smyth et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and cites previous work (Smyth et al., 2002).

claim: Splenocytes from MyD88-deficient mice show killing activity against B16 cells at a rate even slightly higher than those from wild-type mice.
source: Although IRF5 is best known as a transcription factor activated by TLR signaling, we observed that splenocytes from mice deficient in MyD88, the common adapter for all TLRs, shows killing activity against B16 cells at a rate even slightly higher than those from WT mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro killing assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Dectin-1 is widely expressed by dendritic cells and macrophages.
source: In fact, Dectin-1, known to recognize β-glucans of fungal cell wall (Brown, 2006), is widely expressed by DCs and macrophages and the activation of IRF5 by the Dectin-1-Syk pathway has been implicated in the induction of type I interferon-β (IFN-β) gene upon fungal infection (del Fresno et al., 2013; Leibundgut-Landmann et al., 2008; Backer et al., 2008; Brown et al., 2002; Honda and Taniguchi, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Brown, 2006; del Fresno et al., 2013; Leibundgut-Landmann et al., 2008; Backer et al., 2008; Brown et al., 2002; Honda and Taniguchi, 2006).

claim: Dectin-1 recognizes β-glucans of fungal cell wall.
source: In fact, Dectin-1, known to recognize β-glucans of fungal cell wall (Brown, 2006), is widely expressed by DCs and macrophages and the activation of IRF5 by the Dectin-1-Syk pathway has been implicated in the induction of type I interferon-β (IFN-β) gene upon fungal infection (del Fresno et al., 2013; Leibundgut-Landmann et al., 2008; Backer et al., 2008; Brown et al., 2002; Honda and Taniguchi, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Brown, 2006).

claim: The activation of IRF5 by the Dectin-1-Syk pathway has been implicated in the induction of type I interferon-β (IFN-β) gene upon fungal infection.
source: In fact, Dectin-1, known to recognize β-glucans of fungal cell wall (Brown, 2006), is widely expressed by DCs and macrophages and the activation of IRF5 by the Dectin-1-Syk pathway has been implicated in the induction of type I interferon-β (IFN-β) gene upon fungal infection (del Fresno et al., 2013; Leibundgut-Landmann et al., 2008; Backer et al., 2008; Brown et al., 2002; Honda and Taniguchi, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (del Fresno et al., 2013; Leibundgut-Landmann et al., 2008; Backer et al., 2008; Brown et al., 2002; Honda and Taniguchi, 2006).

claim: Nuclear translocation of IRF5 occurs in wild-type splenocytes following incubation with B16 cells.
source: Interestingly, we observed nuclear translocation of IRF5, a hallmark of its activation (Honda and Taniguchi, 2006), following incubation of WT splenocytes with B16 cells (in 50 to 1 or 100 to 1 cell ratio), but not in splenocytes from mice deficient in the Clec7a gene that encodes Dectin-1 (hereafter Dectin-1-deficient mice), indicating there is a Dectin-1 signal-dependent IRF5 activation by the tumor cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and cites previous work (Honda and Taniguchi, 2006).

claim: Nuclear translocation of IRF5 does not occur in Dectin-1-deficient splenocytes following incubation with B16 cells.
source: Interestingly, we observed nuclear translocation of IRF5, a hallmark of its activation (Honda and Taniguchi, 2006), following incubation of WT splenocytes with B16 cells (in 50 to 1 or 100 to 1 cell ratio), but not in splenocytes from mice deficient in the Clec7a gene that encodes Dectin-1 (hereafter Dectin-1-deficient mice), indicating there is a Dectin-1 signal-dependent IRF5 activation by the tumor cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There is a Dectin-1 signal-dependent IRF5 activation by B16 tumor cells.
source: Interestingly, we observed nuclear translocation of IRF5, a hallmark of its activation (Honda and Taniguchi, 2006), following incubation of WT splenocytes with B16 cells (in 50 to 1 or 100 to 1 cell ratio), but not in splenocytes from mice deficient in the Clec7a gene that encodes Dectin-1 (hereafter Dectin-1-deficient mice), indicating there is a Dectin-1 signal-dependent IRF5 activation by the tumor cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing IRF5 nuclear translocation in WT but not Dectin-1-deficient splenocytes.

claim: IRF5 activation by B16 cells is not inhibited by FK506.
source: Of note, IRF5 activation by B16 cells was not inhibited by FK506, suggesting there is a calcineurin-independent pathway for this activation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is a calcineurin-independent pathway for IRF5 activation by B16 cells.
source: Of note, IRF5 activation by B16 cells was not inhibited by FK506, suggesting there is a calcineurin-independent pathway for this activation (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing that FK506 does not inhibit IRF5 activation.

claim: Dectin-1-deficient splenocytes show dramatically reduced in vitro tumoricidal activity against B16 cells.
source: Consistent with the above notion, a dramatic reduction of in vitro tumoricidal activity was observed with Dectin-1-deficient splenocytes (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro killing assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Purified NK cells from Dectin-1-deficient mice show a slight decrease in cell killing activity against B16 cells compared to wild-type NK cells.
source: When NK cells were purified from WT and Dectin-1-deficient splenocytes and subjected to the in vitro killing assay for B16 cells, a slight decrease in cell killing activity of Dectin-1-defcient NK cells was seen as compared to WT NK cells, indicating an ancillary role of the B16-Dectin-1 signaling in NK cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro killing assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Dectin-1 mRNA is expressed in NK cells and other innate immune cells.
source: Dectin-1 mRNA expression was indeed observed in NK cells and other innate immune cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B,C); however, Dectin-1 expression in NK cells does not account for the above Dectin-1-IRF5 axis as IRF5-deficient NK cells show normal cell killing activity (Figure 1C; middle panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B,C.

claim: Dectin-1 expression in NK cells does not account for the Dectin-1-IRF5 axis in NK cell-mediated killing.
source: Dectin-1 mRNA expression was indeed observed in NK cells and other innate immune cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B,C); however, Dectin-1 expression in NK cells does not account for the above Dectin-1-IRF5 axis as IRF5-deficient NK cells show normal cell killing activity (Figure 1C; middle panel).
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing that IRF5-deficient NK cells have normal killing activity despite Dectin-1 expression.

claim: CD11b+ or CD11c+ cells from Dectin-1-deficient mice show marked reduction of NK killing activity in co-culture assays compared to those from wild-type mice.
source: When WT-derived resting NK cells were purified and subjected to the co-culture assay, a marked reduction of NK killing activity was also observed when Dectin-1-deficient CD11b+ or CD11c+ cells were used in lieu of those from WT mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from co-culture assays shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The reduction of NK cell killing activity is more pronounced when CD11b+ or CD11c+ cells from Dectin-1-deficient mice are used compared to those from IRF5-deficient mice.
source: It is worth noting that, consistent with the results showing the existence of IRF5-independent pathway for the Dectin-1 signaling, the reduction of NK cell killing activity was even more pronounced when CD11b+ or CD11c+ cells from Dectin-1-deficient mice were subjected to the co-culture assay compared to those from IRF5-deficient mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from co-culture assays shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: There is an IRF5-independent pathway for Dectin-1 signaling.
source: It is worth noting that, consistent with the results showing the existence of IRF5-independent pathway for the Dectin-1 signaling, the reduction of NK cell killing activity was even more pronounced when CD11b+ or CD11c+ cells from Dectin-1-deficient mice were subjected to the co-culture assay compared to those from IRF5-deficient mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing differential effects of Dectin-1 and IRF5 deficiency on NK cell killing activity.

claim: Dectin-1 on dendritic cells and/or macrophages is involved in the full-blown NK-mediated tumoricidal activity.
source: These observations in toto underscore the involvement of Dectin-1 on DCs and/or macrophages in the full-blown NK-mediated tumoricidal activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental observations showing the role of Dectin-1 in DCs and macrophages.

claim: Additional innate immune receptor(s) may contribute to NK cell activation by CD11b+ or CD11c+ cells.
source: On the other hand, since the NK cell-enhancing activity is not totally abrogated by the absence of Dectin-1 in CD11b+ or CD11c+ cells (Figure 2C), there is perhaps contribution of additional innate immune receptor(s) in these cells for NK cell activation ('Discussion').
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing that Dectin-1 deficiency does not completely abolish NK cell-enhancing activity.

claim: Dectin-1-deficient mice show marked enhancement of metastasis of B16 cells in the lungs compared to wild-type mice.
source: As shown in Figure 2D,E, a marked enhancement of metastasis of B16 cells was seen in the lungs of Dectin-1-deficient mice as compared with those of WT mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from lung metastasis assays shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: Loss of tumor growth control occurs when Dectin-1-deficient mice are inoculated subcutaneously with B16 cells.
source: Loss of tumor growth control also occurred when Dectin-1-deficient mice were inoculated subcutaneously with B16 cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The metastasis to the lung in Dectin-1-deficient mice is significantly more profound than that observed in IRF5-deficient mice.
source: Of note, the metastasis to the lung was significantly more profound than that observed in IRF5-deficient mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 5); this observation is consistent with the above in vitro data, which shows that the IRF5 pathway contributes partly to Dectin-1 signaling (Figure 2C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: The IRF5 pathway contributes partly to Dectin-1 signaling.
source: Of note, the metastasis to the lung was significantly more profound than that observed in IRF5-deficient mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 5); this observation is consistent with the above in vitro data, which shows that the IRF5 pathway contributes partly to Dectin-1 signaling (Figure 2C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data comparing Dectin-1 and IRF5 deficiency effects.

claim: The control of lung metastasis of B16 cells is equally lost between wild-type and Dectin-1-deficient mice when NK cells are depleted prior to tumor challenge.
source: In addition, the control of lung metastasis of B16 cells is equally lost between WT and Dectin-1-deficient mice when NK cells were depleted prior to tumor challenge (Figure 2—figure supplement 6); this result further supports the notion that NK cells are indeed the effector cells and that they need the assistance of DCs and macrophages for which Dectin-1 signaling is critical, in the orchestration for the innate control of tumor cells in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: NK cells are the effector cells in the innate control of tumor cells in vivo.
source: In addition, the control of lung metastasis of B16 cells is equally lost between WT and Dectin-1-deficient mice when NK cells were depleted prior to tumor challenge (Figure 2—figure supplement 6); this result further supports the notion that NK cells are indeed the effector cells and that they need the assistance of DCs and macrophages for which Dectin-1 signaling is critical, in the orchestration for the innate control of tumor cells in vivo.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing that NK cell depletion abolishes tumor control in both WT and Dectin-1-deficient mice.

claim: NK cells need the assistance of dendritic cells and macrophages for which Dectin-1 signaling is critical in the orchestration for the innate control of tumor cells in vivo.
source: In addition, the control of lung metastasis of B16 cells is equally lost between WT and Dectin-1-deficient mice when NK cells were depleted prior to tumor challenge (Figure 2—figure supplement 6); this result further supports the notion that NK cells are indeed the effector cells and that they need the assistance of DCs and macrophages for which Dectin-1 signaling is critical, in the orchestration for the innate control of tumor cells in vivo.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing the role of Dectin-1 in DCs and macrophages for NK cell-mediated tumor control.

claim: No overt difference was observed between wild-type and Dectin-1-deficient mice in the proportion of splenic NK cells.
source: It is worth noting that no overt difference was observed between WT and Dectin-1-deficient mice in terms of (i) the proportion of splenic NK cells, (ii) production of IFN-γ by NK cells in vitro, and (iii) NK cell-dependent clearance of murine cytomegalovirus (MCMV) in vivo (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: No overt difference was observed between wild-type and Dectin-1-deficient mice in production of IFN-γ by NK cells in vitro.
source: It is worth noting that no overt difference was observed between WT and Dectin-1-deficient mice in terms of (i) the proportion of splenic NK cells, (ii) production of IFN-γ by NK cells in vitro, and (iii) NK cell-dependent clearance of murine cytomegalovirus (MCMV) in vivo (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: No overt difference was observed between wild-type and Dectin-1-deficient mice in NK cell-dependent clearance of murine cytomegalovirus (MCMV) in vivo.
source: It is worth noting that no overt difference was observed between WT and Dectin-1-deficient mice in terms of (i) the proportion of splenic NK cells, (ii) production of IFN-γ by NK cells in vitro, and (iii) NK cell-dependent clearance of murine cytomegalovirus (MCMV) in vivo (Figure 2—figure supplement 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 7.

claim: NK cell-dependent immune responses are not globally impaired by the absence of Dectin-1; impairment is selective to the anti-tumor response.
source: Therefore, NK cell-dependent immune responses are not globally impaired by the absence of Dectin-1; impairment is selective to the anti-tumor response.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing normal NK cell function in MCMV clearance but impaired anti-tumor response in Dectin-1-deficient mice.

claim: Soluble Dectin-1 (sDectin-1) binds substantially to B16 cells.
source: Interestingly, substantial binding of sDectin-1 to B16 cells was detected, whereas binding was almost undetectable to mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) and other primary, non-transformed cells (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from sDectin-1 binding assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Soluble Dectin-1 (sDectin-1) binding is almost undetectable to mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) and other primary, non-transformed cells.
source: Interestingly, substantial binding of sDectin-1 to B16 cells was detected, whereas binding was almost undetectable to mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEFs) and other primary, non-transformed cells (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from sDectin-1 binding assays shown in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: N-glycosidase treatment markedly reduces sDectin-1 binding to B16 cells.
source: Interestingly, we found that sDectin-1 binding to B16 cells was markedly reduced upon N-glycosidase treatment, while treatment by O-glycosidase or neuraminidase showed only a marginal effect, suggesting there is a major requirement for N-glycan structures to Dectin-1 binding (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from sDectin-1 binding assays shown in Figure 3B.

claim: O-glycosidase or neuraminidase treatment shows only a marginal effect on sDectin-1 binding to B16 cells.
source: Interestingly, we found that sDectin-1 binding to B16 cells was markedly reduced upon N-glycosidase treatment, while treatment by O-glycosidase or neuraminidase showed only a marginal effect, suggesting there is a major requirement for N-glycan structures to Dectin-1 binding (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from sDectin-1 binding assays shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is a major requirement for N-glycan structures for Dectin-1 binding to B16 cells.
source: Interestingly, we found that sDectin-1 binding to B16 cells was markedly reduced upon N-glycosidase treatment, while treatment by O-glycosidase or neuraminidase showed only a marginal effect, suggesting there is a major requirement for N-glycan structures to Dectin-1 binding (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing that N-glycosidase treatment reduces sDectin-1 binding.

claim: N-glycosidase pretreatment of B16 cells results in marked reduction of tumoricidal activity of splenocytes.
source: Consistent with this, a marked reduction of tumoricidal activity of splenocytes was observed when B16 cells were pretreated with N-glycosidase, whereas O-glycosidase treatment did not affect this activity (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro killing assays shown in Figure 3C.

claim: O-glycosidase treatment of B16 cells does not affect tumoricidal activity of splenocytes.
source: Consistent with this, a marked reduction of tumoricidal activity of splenocytes was observed when B16 cells were pretreated with N-glycosidase, whereas O-glycosidase treatment did not affect this activity (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro killing assays shown in Figure 3C.

claim: N-glycosidase treatment of B16 cells does not affect the in vitro killing activity of purified NK cells.
source: Further, N-glycosidase treatment of B16 cells did not affect the in vitro killing activity of purified NK cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), indicating in toto there is a critical role of Dectin-1 recognition of and signaling by N-glycan structures on tumor cells by DCs and macrophages.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro killing assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: There is a critical role of Dectin-1 recognition of and signaling by N-glycan structures on tumor cells by dendritic cells and macrophages.
source: Further, N-glycosidase treatment of B16 cells did not affect the in vitro killing activity of purified NK cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), indicating in toto there is a critical role of Dectin-1 recognition of and signaling by N-glycan structures on tumor cells by DCs and macrophages.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing differential effects of N-glycosidase treatment on splenocytes versus purified NK cells.

claim: N-glycan structures such as N-glycans with β1,6-GlcNAc branching are detected on B16 cells.
source: As reported previously, N-glycan structures, such as N-glycans with β1,6-GlcNAc branching (Fernandes et al., 1991), the expression of which is increased in tumor cells, were detected.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry analysis and cites previous work (Fernandes et al., 1991).

claim: The expression of N-glycans with β1,6-GlcNAc branching is increased in tumor cells.
source: As reported previously, N-glycan structures, such as N-glycans with β1,6-GlcNAc branching (Fernandes et al., 1991), the expression of which is increased in tumor cells, were detected.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Fernandes et al., 1991).

claim: Pretreatment of the supernatant by sDectin-1 did not alter the mass spectrometry peak pattern of N-glycan structures.
source: Of note, pretreatment of the supernatant by sDectin-1 did not alter the MS peak pattern (Figure 3—figure supplements 4–6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 4–6.

claim: N-glycan structures need to be bound to proteins for Dectin-1 recognition.
source: This observation suggests that N-glycan structures, highly expressed in tumor cells, need to be bound to proteins for the Dectin-1 recognition (See below).
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing that sDectin-1 does not bind free N-glycans in solution.

claim: Supernatants from CD11b+ or CD11c+ cells mixed with B16 cells have little, if any, effect on NK cell activity.
source: To address the issue of whether Dectin-1 signaling is required for direct cell-to-cell contact or for the induction of a soluble mediator(s), we examined supernatants from CD11b+ or CD11c+ cells mixed with B16 cells and found that they had little, if any, effect on NK cell activity (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Antibodies against type I IFNs or IL12 show no effect on the NK cell-enhancing activity by dendritic cells.
source: In addition, the use of antibodies against type I IFNs or IL12, both cytokines are known to activate NK cells (Degli-Esposti and Smyth, 2005), showed no effect on the NK cell-enhancing activity by DCs (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and cites previous work (Degli-Esposti and Smyth, 2005).

claim: Dectin-1 signaling is crucial for mediating cell-to-cell contact and subsequent NK activation.
source: These results support the notion that Dectin-1 signaling is crucial for mediating cell-to-cell contact and subsequent NK activation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing that soluble factors and cytokine antibodies do not affect NK cell-enhancing activity.

claim: Inam (Fam26f) mRNA is induced in wild-type dendritic cells co-cultured with B16 cells in a Dectin-1-dependent manner.
source: The affected genes include several membrane-bound proteins amongst which Inam (termed as Fam26f) is known to activate NK cells via its homophilic interaction (Ebihara et al., 2010). Interestingly, the Inam mRNA induction by B16 cells is IRF5-dependent in splenic CD11c+ cells (Figure 4D) and lentiviral expression of INAM cDNA in bone marrow-derived DCs resulted in the enhancement of NK cell-mediated killing of B16 cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from microarray and qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 4C,D and cites previous work (Ebihara et al., 2010).

claim: Inam (Fam26f) is known to activate NK cells via its homophilic interaction.
source: The affected genes include several membrane-bound proteins amongst which Inam (termed as Fam26f) is known to activate NK cells via its homophilic interaction (Ebihara et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Ebihara et al., 2010).

claim: Inam mRNA induction by B16 cells is IRF5-dependent in splenic CD11c+ cells.
source: Interestingly, the Inam mRNA induction by B16 cells is IRF5-dependent in splenic CD11c+ cells (Figure 4D) and lentiviral expression of INAM cDNA in bone marrow-derived DCs resulted in the enhancement of NK cell-mediated killing of B16 cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Lentiviral expression of INAM cDNA in bone marrow-derived dendritic cells results in the enhancement of NK cell-mediated killing of B16 cells.
source: Interestingly, the Inam mRNA induction by B16 cells is IRF5-dependent in splenic CD11c+ cells (Figure 4D) and lentiviral expression of INAM cDNA in bone marrow-derived DCs resulted in the enhancement of NK cell-mediated killing of B16 cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro killing assays shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The Dectin-1-IRF5-INAM pathway may participate in the dendritic cell-mediated activation of NK cells, at least in part.
source: Thus, the Dectin-1-IRF5-INAM pathway may participate in the DC-mediated activation of NK cells, at least in part, in this experimental setting.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing Dectin-1-dependent Inam induction and INAM-mediated NK cell activation.

claim: Soluble Dectin-1 (sDectin-1) binding capacity is strong for 3LL (lung carcinoma), YAC-1 (lymphoma), and Meth-A (fibrosarcoma) cell lines.
source: The binding capacity was variable in that the binding was strong for 3LL (lung carcinoma), YAC-1 (lymphoma), and Meth-A (fibrosarcoma) cell lines, but was significantly weaker for some tumor cells such as SL4 (colon carcinoma) and B16F10 (melanoma) cell lines (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from sDectin-1 binding assays shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Soluble Dectin-1 (sDectin-1) binding capacity is significantly weaker for SL4 (colon carcinoma) and B16F10 (melanoma) cell lines.
source: The binding capacity was variable in that the binding was strong for 3LL (lung carcinoma), YAC-1 (lymphoma), and Meth-A (fibrosarcoma) cell lines, but was significantly weaker for some tumor cells such as SL4 (colon carcinoma) and B16F10 (melanoma) cell lines (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from sDectin-1 binding assays shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: SL4 and B16F10 cell lines are known to metastasize massively even in wild-type mice.
source: It is worth noting that the latter two cell lines are known to metastasize massively even in WT mice (Morimoto-Tomita et al., 2005) (See below).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to previous work (Morimoto-Tomita et al., 2005).

claim: Chemical cross-linking of sDectin-1 generates multiple smear bands of similar pattern using B16F1 and 3LL cells.
source: In addition, chemical cross-linking of sDectin-1, followed by immunoblot analysis, generated multiple smear bands of similar pattern using B16F1 and 3LL cells, whereas bands were barely detectable with B16F10 cells or MEFs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from chemical cross-linking and immunoblot analysis.

claim: Chemical cross-linking of sDectin-1 generates bands that are barely detectable with B16F10 cells or MEFs.
source: In addition, chemical cross-linking of sDectin-1, followed by immunoblot analysis, generated multiple smear bands of similar pattern using B16F1 and 3LL cells, whereas bands were barely detectable with B16F10 cells or MEFs.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from chemical cross-linking and immunoblot analysis.

claim: The bands generated by chemical cross-linking of sDectin-1 are abolished by pretreatment of cells with N-glycosidase.
source: Further, these bands are abolished by the pretreatment of cells with N-glycosidase (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Similar or identical N-glycan structures are expressed on multiple proteins that function as Dectin-1 ligands in B16F1, 3LL, and probably other Dectin-1 binding tumor cells.
source: Thus, these data suggest that similar or identical N-glycan structures are expressed on multiple proteins that function as Dectin-1 ligands in these, and probably other, Dectin-1 binding tumor cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing similar cross-linking patterns and N-glycosidase sensitivity.

claim: Dectin-1-dependent cell killing activity is observed against 3LL and YAC-1 cells.
source: We observed Dectin1-dependent cell killing activity against 3LL and YAC-1 cells (Figure 5B; left panel and Figure 5—figure supplement 3), whereas the killing activity of WT splenocytes against SL4 cells was significantly weaker as compared to that for 3LL or YAC-1 cells and was reduced only marginally in Dectin-1-deficient splenocytes (Figure 5B; right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro killing assays shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The killing activity of wild-type splenocytes against SL4 cells is significantly weaker compared to that for 3LL or YAC-1 cells.
source: We observed Dectin1-dependent cell killing activity against 3LL and YAC-1 cells (Figure 5B; left panel and Figure 5—figure supplement 3), whereas the killing activity of WT splenocytes against SL4 cells was significantly weaker as compared to that for 3LL or YAC-1 cells and was reduced only marginally in Dectin-1-deficient splenocytes (Figure 5B; right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro killing assays shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The killing activity of wild-type splenocytes against SL4 cells is reduced only marginally in Dectin-1-deficient splenocytes.
source: We observed Dectin1-dependent cell killing activity against 3LL and YAC-1 cells (Figure 5B; left panel and Figure 5—figure supplement 3), whereas the killing activity of WT splenocytes against SL4 cells was significantly weaker as compared to that for 3LL or YAC-1 cells and was reduced only marginally in Dectin-1-deficient splenocytes (Figure 5B; right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vitro killing assays shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Tumor cells expressing Dectin-1 ligands at high levels are more susceptible to NK cell-mediated killing in a manner dependent on Dectin-1 signaling.
source: These results support the notion that tumor cells expressing Dectin-1 ligands at high levels are more susceptible to NK cell-mediated killing in a manner dependent on Dectin-1 signaling.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing correlation between sDectin-1 binding and Dectin-1-dependent killing activity.

claim: Marked enhancement of lung metastasis of 3LL cells is observed in Dectin-1-deficient mice but not in wild-type mice.
source: As shown in Figure 5C, a marked enhancement of lung metastasis of 3LL cells was observed in Dectin-1-deficient mice, but not in WT mice (Figure 5C; left panel), while SL4 cells without significant sDectin-1 binding (Figure 5A; right panel) underwent massive metastasis in both WT and mutant mice (Figure 5C; right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from lung metastasis assays shown in Figure 5C.

claim: SL4 cells undergo massive metastasis in both wild-type and Dectin-1-deficient mice.
source: As shown in Figure 5C, a marked enhancement of lung metastasis of 3LL cells was observed in Dectin-1-deficient mice, but not in WT mice (Figure 5C; left panel), while SL4 cells without significant sDectin-1 binding (Figure 5A; right panel) underwent massive metastasis in both WT and mutant mice (Figure 5C; right panel).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from lung metastasis assays shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Massive metastasis of B16F10 cells is observed without significant difference between wild-type and Dectin-1-deficient mice.
source: Expectedly, massive metastasis of B16F10 cells was observed without significant difference between WT and Dectin-1-deficient mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 4), suggesting that B16F10 cells could have been selected to evade the Dectin-1-mediated anti-tumor orchestration.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from lung metastasis assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: B16F10 cells could have been selected to evade the Dectin-1-mediated anti-tumor orchestration.
source: Expectedly, massive metastasis of B16F10 cells was observed without significant difference between WT and Dectin-1-deficient mice (Figure 5—figure supplement 4), suggesting that B16F10 cells could have been selected to evade the Dectin-1-mediated anti-tumor orchestration.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from experimental data showing lack of Dectin-1-dependent control of B16F10 metastasis.

claim: The recognition of and signaling by Dectin-1 in dendritic cells and macrophages constitute a critical aspect of the NK cell-mediated anti-tumor innate immunity.
source: Thus, these in vivo observations are consistent with in vitro observations in that the recognition of and signaling by Dectin-1 in DCs and macrophages constitute a critical aspect of the NK cell-mediated anti-tumor innate immunity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental observations showing the role of Dectin-1 in DCs and macrophages for NK cell-mediated tumor control.

claim: Human soluble Dectin-1 binds to several human tumor cell lines.
source: Finally, Dectin-1 binding to human tumor cell lines was examined by preparing a human sDectin-1. Interestingly, we found human sDectin-1 binds to several of these cell lines (Figure 5—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from sDectin-1 binding assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5.

claim: Dectin-1-dependent induction of Inam mRNA occurs in mouse dendritic cells by human cancer cell line HBC4.
source: We also observed the Dectin-1-dependent induction of Inam mRNA in mouse DCs by human cancer cell line HBC4, to which human sDectin-1 strongly binds (Figure 5—figure supplement 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 6.

claim: Mouse dendritic cells respond to human Dectin-1 ligands for gene induction.
source: Since mouse and human Dectin-1 are highly conserved, we infer the mouse DCs respond to human Dectin-1 ligands for gene induction.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing mouse DC response to human cancer cells and knowledge of Dectin-1 conservation.

claim: A similar or identical anti-tumor Dectin-1 signaling mechanism exists in the human immune system.
source: As such, these results suggest the presence of a similar or identical anti-tumor Dectin-1 signaling mechanism in the human immune system.
evidence: The claim is inferred from experimental data showing human sDectin-1 binding to human tumor cells and mouse DC response to human cancer cells.

claim: The innate immune receptor Dectin-1 expressed on dendritic cells and macrophages is important to NK-mediated killing of tumor cells.
source: In the present study, we demonstrated that the innate immune receptor Dectin-1 expressed on DCs and macrophages is important to NK-mediated killing of tumor cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental observations throughout the study.

claim: NK cells are required to orchestrate with dendritic cells and macrophages for cell killing, wherein activation of the IRF5 transcription factor by Dectin-1 signaling instigated by receptor recognition of N-glycan structures on tumor cells is critical.
source: Our results indicate that NK cells are required to orchestrate with DCs and macrophages for cell killing, wherein activation of the IRF5 transcription factor by Dectin-1 signaling instigated by receptor recognition of N-glycan structures on tumor cells is critical.
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple experimental observations throughout the study.

claim: Excessive growth of tumors with sDectin-1 binding occurs in mice genetically deficient in either Dectin-1 or IRF5 in vivo.
source: This notion is supported by an excessive growth of tumors with sDectin-1 binding in mice genetically deficient in either Dectin-1 or IRF5 in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from in vivo tumor growth assays.

claim: This is the first demonstration that an innate immune receptor contributes to anti-tumor recognition and signaling through orchestration of innate immune cells.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that an innate immune receptor contributes to anti-tumor recognition and signaling through orchestration of innate immune cells.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the field and the novelty of their findings.

claim: Enhanced glycosylation levels provide growth advantages to many if not all tumor cells.
source: In this context, it has been shown that enhanced glycosylation levels provide growth advantages to many if not all tumor cells (Granovsky et al., 2000; Gu and Taniguchi, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous work (Granovsky et al., 2000; Gu and Taniguchi, 2008).

claim: Dectin-1 recognition of and activation by N-glycan structures may be contingent on the absolute expression levels of N-glycans and/or their associated proteins on the cell.
source: Obviously further work will be required to discern the detailed nature of the ligands, it is possible that Dectin-1 recognition of and activation by N-glycan structures are contingent on the absolute expression levels of N-glycans and/or their associated proteins on the cell; that is, tumor cells with 'increased self' molecules are targets for innate recognition for activation of the immune system.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from experimental observations.

claim: Dectin-1 recognition may require particular, tumor-specific N-glycan-containing structures, which may belong to 'altered self'.
source: However, it is also possible that Dectin-1 recognition requires particular, tumor-specific N-glycan-containing structures, which may belong to 'altered self' (Medzhitov and Janeway, 2002).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from experimental observations and cites previous work (Medzhitov and Janeway, 2002).

claim: Dectin-1-binding structures may fit into the category of 'tumor-associated molecular patterns (TAMPs)' vis-à-vis PAMPs for invading pathogens and DAMPs for normal cells subjected to stress or death.
source: Whichever the case, Dectin-1-binding structures may fit into the category of 'tumor-associated molecular patterns (TAMPs)' vis-à-vis PAMPs for invading pathogens and DAMPs for normal cells subjected to stress or death (Rubartelli and Lotze, 2007; Kawai and Akira, 2010).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from experimental observations and cites previous work (Rubartelli and Lotze, 2007; Kawai and Akira, 2010).

claim: Other C-type lectin receptors may be involved in the orchestration of innate immune cells for the efficient NK cell-mediated anti-tumor immune response.
source: Our data showing that Dectin-1-deficiency does not entirely abrogate the NK-enhancing activity of CD11b+ or CD11c+ cells suggests the interesting possibility that other CLRs are also involved in the orchestration of innate immune cells for the efficient NK cell-mediated anti-tumor immune response.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from experimental data showing incomplete abrogation of NK-enhancing activity in Dectin-1-deficient cells.

claim: The host's innate system could have evolved to limit the immune evasion of tumor development through recognition of glycosylation products via Dectin-1 and other C-type lectin receptor family members.
source: It is curious that in many tumor cells glycosylation levels are generally enhanced, providing an advantage to tumor cells in migration and metastasis (Granovsky et al., 2000; Gu and Taniguchi, 2008). If so, the host's innate system could have evolved to limit the immune evasion of tumor development through recognition of glycosylation products via Dectin-1 and other CLR family members.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from experimental observations and cites previous work (Granovsky et al., 2000; Gu and Taniguchi, 2008).

claim: Dectin-1 mRNA is expressed in CD11b+ or CD11c+ cells from liver and lung.
source: It is interesting to note that Dectin-1 mRNA is also expressed in CD11b+ or CD11c+ cells from liver and lung (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C); hence, we infer that Dectin-1 signaling may contribute to the control of tumor progression in various tissues.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Dectin-1 signaling may contribute to the control of tumor progression in various tissues.
source: It is interesting to note that Dectin-1 mRNA is also expressed in CD11b+ or CD11c+ cells from liver and lung (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C); hence, we infer that Dectin-1 signaling may contribute to the control of tumor progression in various tissues.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from experimental data showing Dectin-1 expression in liver and lung immune cells.

claim: Tumor cells show a differential expression profile for Dectin-1 ligands in vivo.
source: In addition, since tumor cells are phenotypically and functionally heterogeneous even within the same tumor mass (Meacham and Morrison, 2013), it is possible that tumor cells show a differential expression profiles for Dectin-1 ligands in vivo.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from knowledge of tumor heterogeneity and cites previous work (Meacham and Morrison, 2013).

claim: NK cells activated by CD11b+ or CD11c+ cells via Dectin-1 signaling may exert tumoricidal activities on tumor cells regardless of their Dectin-1 ligand expression.
source: If so, it may be the case that the in vivo progression of a tumor is controlled via direct and indirect Dectin-1 signaling, that is, NK cells activated by CD11b+ or CD11c+ cells via Dectin-1 signaling may exert tumoricidal activities on tumor cells regardless on their Dectin-1 ligand expression.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from experimental observations.

claim: Other membrane molecules identified in the microarray analysis may participate in the enhancement of NK cells for anti-tumor response.
source: Although our study suggests the involvement of INAM, we infer that other membrane molecules identified here (Figure 4C), which are without a known function at present, may also participate.
evidence: The claim is speculative, inferred from experimental data showing induction of multiple membrane-bound proteins.

claim: Monoclonal antibodies may activate dendritic cells and macrophages via FcRIV-FcRγ pathway to mediate both ADCC and further contribute to NK cell activation through a mechanism similar to the Dectin-1 pathway.
source: As such, Abs may activate DCs and macrophages via FcRIV-FcRγ pathway to mediate both ADCC and further contribute to NK cell activation through a mechanism similar to the pathway we describe in this study.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from experimental observations and knowledge of FcR signaling.

claim: Dectin-1 signaling by tumor recognition may affect adaptive anti-tumor immune responses.
source: Finally, in light of the tenet that innate immunity instructs adaptive immunity (Janeway and Medzhitov, 2002), our study may also raise an interesting issue of whether Dectin-1 signaling by tumor recognition also affects adaptive anti-tumor immune responses, and also may provide new means for the efficient immune responses for cancers such as Dectin-1 agonistic Abs.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from experimental observations and cites previous work (Janeway and Medzhitov, 2002).

claim: Dectin-1 agonistic antibodies may provide new means for efficient immune responses for cancers.
source: Finally, in light of the tenet that innate immunity instructs adaptive immunity (Janeway and Medzhitov, 2002), our study may also raise an interesting issue of whether Dectin-1 signaling by tumor recognition also affects adaptive anti-tumor immune responses, and also may provide new means for the efficient immune responses for cancers such as Dectin-1 agonistic Abs.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from experimental observations.
